facts.statement: The only known fossil of Philovenator is a single left hindlimb discovered in 1988 by the China-Canada Dinosaur Project.
facts.quote: Philovenator is known from a single left hindlimb, first discovered in 1988 by the China-Canada Dinosaur Project.

facts.statement: The name Philovenator literally translates to "love hunter".
facts.quote: Philovenator (literally meaning "love hunter") is an extinct genus of troodontid paravian dinosaurs

facts.statement: Philovenator was a small, bird-like, and gracile member of the troodontid group of maniraptoran dinosaurs.
facts.quote: Philovenator is a troodontid, a group of small, bird-like, gracile maniraptorans.

facts.statement: As a troodontid, Philovenator possessed sickle-claws, raptorial hands, and likely had keen senses and advanced behavior.
facts.quote: Troodontids have sickle-claws and raptorial hands, and some of the highest non-avian encephalization quotients, meaning they were behaviourally advanced and had keen senses.

facts.statement: A distinctive process on the inner side of the lower thighbone was one of the distinguishing traits of Philovenator.
facts.quote: The thighbone possesses a distinctive process at the inner side of the lower end.

facts.statement: The tarsometatarsus of Philovenator was 25% longer than its thighbone and twenty-five times longer than it was wide.
facts.quote: The metatarsus has fused with the lower ankle bones into a very elongated and narrow tarsometatarsus, being 25% longer than the thighbone and twenty-five times longer than wide.

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analysis recovered Philovenator as an advanced troodontid closely related to Saurornithoides, Zanabazar, and Troodon.
facts.quote: Philovenator was recovered as an advanced troodontid, closely related to other Late Cretaceous troodontids, such as Saurornithoides and Zanabazar from Mongolia, and Troodon from North America.

facts.statement: Philovenator belongs to the subfamily Jinfengopteryginae.
The fossil record for Philovenator spans from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Campanian to Campanian (83.6 to 72.2 million years ago)
